concept.name: Modular Monolith Design

relationships.description: Connects Modular Monolith Design to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Structure a single deployable binary into strictly isolated domain modules with enforced public APIs and private schemas—gaining clean boundaries without network tax.
spark.keyTakeaway: Enforce module boundaries at compile/test time (ArchUnit, Spring Modulith, import-linter) and isolate database schemas so any module can be extracted into a microservice later in days, not months.

concept.whyItMatters: Teams often jump straight from a tangled 'Big Ball of Mud' monolith to microservices, trading code coupling for distributed systems complexity. A modular monolith delivers strict domain isolation, single-transaction ACID guarantees, and sub-microsecond in-process calls while keeping operations down to one CI/CD pipeline.
whenToUse: Engineering organizations of 5–60 developers building a rich domain where boundaries are still evolving.
Core workflows benefit from single-database ACID transactions and low-latency (<1 ms) cross-module reads without network serialization.
You want an evolutionary 'microservices-ready' architecture without paying the Kubernetes, Istio, and distributed debugging tax today.
whenNotToUse: Modules require genuinely incompatible runtimes or hardware (e.g., Python/PyTorch GPU inference alongside a Rust high-frequency proxy).
Independent scaling or strict compliance isolation (e.g., PCI-DSS cardholder vault) requires physical process and network separation.
Teams exceed ~80–100 engineers and hit hard Git merge-queue or single-binary build-time limits even with modular builds.
keyPoints: Organize packages by business capability/vertical slice (`orders`, `inventory`, `billing`), never by technical layer (`controllers`, `services`, `repositories`).
Expose a narrow public module API (facade + DTOs + domain events) and keep entities, repositories, and helpers package-private/internal.
Enforce zero illegal cross-module imports in CI using fitness functions like ArchUnit (Java), Spring Modulith, or `import-linter` (Python).
Give each module its own logical PostgreSQL schema (`orders.*`, `inventory.*`) and forbid cross-schema foreign keys or SQL joins.
Communicate state changes between modules via an in-process event bus (backed by a transactional outbox if durability/retries are needed).

examples.title: Shopify's Modular Monolith Refactor
examples.scenario: Shopify's core Rails monolith grew to millions of lines with circular dependencies across billing, shipping, and storefront logic.
examples.outcome: Using Packwerk to enforce explicit package boundaries and private constants allowed 1,000+ developers to ship safely in one deployable unit while selectively extracting only high-scale edges.

examples.title: Spring Modulith + PostgreSQL Schemas in FinTech
examples.scenario: A 25-engineer lending startup struggled with 9 microservices that required 2-hour local Docker Compose startups and frequent Saga bugs.
examples.outcome: Consolidating into a Spring Modulith binary with 5 schema-isolated modules cut local test runs from 14 minutes to 38 seconds, eliminated 400 lines of Kafka boilerplate, and reduced p99 loan origination latency by 65%.

tradeOffs.factor: In-Process Call Speed vs. Blast-Radius Isolation
tradeOffs.pro: Cross-module calls execute in ~50 nanoseconds with zero JSON/Protobuf serialization or network failures.
tradeOffs.con: An unhandled OOM or infinite loop in one module can crash the entire process and take down all co-located modules.

tradeOffs.factor: Single ACID Transaction vs. Future Extraction Friction
tradeOffs.pro: Modules sharing one database can participate in a single ACID commit when needed.
tradeOffs.con: If you rely heavily on cross-module ACID transactions, extracting a module later still requires rewriting them into Sagas.

tradeOffs.pro: One CI pipeline, one Docker image, and atomic rollbacks eliminate distributed version skew.
tradeOffs.con: You cannot scale CPU/memory for one hot module independently without scaling the whole binary.

failureModes.name: Boundary Erosion (Accidental Spaghetti)
failureModes.description: Under deadline pressure, a developer imports another module's internal ORM entity directly, re-creating a Big Ball of Mud.
failureModes.mitigation: Fail the CI build automatically using ArchUnit (`@ApplicationModuleTest`), Packwerk, or `import-linter` rules.

failureModes.name: Database-Level Coupling
failureModes.description: Code boundaries look clean, but Module A runs SQL `JOIN`s against Module B's tables, locking both schemas together.
failureModes.mitigation: Separate modules into distinct PostgreSQL schemas with least-privilege DB roles or enforce schema-prefix linting.

failureModes.name: Synchronous Event-Bus Cascades
failureModes.description: Publishing an in-process event triggers 5 synchronous listeners inside the HTTP request thread, spiking latency and causing deadlocks.
failureModes.mitigation: Run cross-module event listeners asynchronously after transaction commit (`@TransactionalEventListener` + outbox table).

failureModes.name: Shared 'Common/Core' Dumping Ground
failureModes.description: A `shared-kernel` module accumulates 40% of the domain entities, coupling every module to it.
failureModes.mitigation: Restrict shared code strictly to primitives, clock/ID utilities, and published event contracts; duplicate small DTOs rather than sharing entities.

commonMistakes: Grouping code into `models/`, `services/`, and `controllers/` at the top level instead of domain module folders.
Returning JPA/SQLAlchemy ORM entities from a module's public facade instead of immutable DTOs.
Allowing circular dependencies (`Orders -> Inventory -> Orders`) instead of breaking cycles with domain events.
Relying on developer discipline alone rather than automated CI architecture tests.
Using the same database connection pool without per-module query timeouts, letting one bad query starve all modules.

sections.content:
## The idea

A **modular monolith** combines the **logical decoupling** of microservices with the **physical simplicity** of a single deployable artifact. Every domain capability lives in a self-contained module with an explicit public facade, private internal implementation, and its own logical database schema. Because all modules run in the same process, cross-module calls happen in nanoseconds—yet automated architecture tests enforce strict boundaries so that extracting any module into a standalone microservice later requires swapping an in-process interface for an RPC/event adapter.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider structuring an e-commerce backend using **Spring Modulith** (Java) or **import-linter** (Python) over PostgreSQL:

1. **Vertical Package Layout**: Top-level packages are `com.app.orders`, `com.app.inventory`, and `com.app.billing`. Inside `orders`, only `OrdersFacade` and `OrderPlacedEvent` are public; `OrderEntity` and `OrderRepository` live in `orders.internal`.
2. **Compile/Test Boundary Gate**: An ArchUnit test runs in CI (`ApplicationModules.of(App.class).verify()`). If `billing` imports `orders.internal.OrderEntity`, the build fails immediately.
3. **Logical Schema Isolation**: PostgreSQL hosts `orders.orders`, `inventory.stock`, and `billing.invoices`. Foreign keys across schemas are forbidden; `billing` stores `order_id` as an opaque UUID.
4. **Post-Commit Async Events**: When `OrdersFacade.placeOrder()` commits, Spring Modulith persists `OrderPlacedEvent` in `orders.event_publication` in the same transaction and dispatches it asynchronously to `inventory` and `billing`.

data.caption: Strict package facades, CI fitness functions, and isolated DB schemas keep modules decoupled inside a single deployable binary.

sections.content:
## Automated architectural fitness functions

Boundaries without enforcement decay within weeks. Bake three automated checks into every PR:

- **Dependency Acyclicity**: `import-linter` (Python) or ArchUnit (Java) verifies zero cycles between top-level domain modules in <5 seconds.
- **Internal Encapsulation**: Only classes/functions in the module root or explicit `api/` package may be imported externally; `internal/` packages are off-limits.
- **Schema Linting**: A migration linter (e.g., Squawk or custom SQL check) rejects `REFERENCES` foreign keys or `JOIN`s crossing schema namespaces.

sections.eyebrow: 04 / Monolith vs. modular monolith vs. microservices
sections.content:
## Monolith vs. modular monolith vs. microservices

| Dimension | Big Ball of Mud | Modular Monolith | Microservices |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Call Latency** | ~50 ns (in-process) | ~50 ns (in-process) | 1–10 ms (gRPC/HTTP + serde) |
| **Boundary Enforcement** | None | CI fitness functions (ArchUnit/Packwerk) | Physical network & separate repos |
| **Data Isolation** | Shared tables & joins | Isolated DB schemas per module | Separate DB instances |
| **Operational Overhead** | Low (1 pipeline) | Low (1 pipeline) | High (K8s, mesh, tracing, N pipelines) |
| **Extraction Cost** | Very high (months) | Low (swap facade for RPC client) | Already extracted |

## Failure modes

Even well-structured modular monoliths can hit operational ceilings:

- **Shared Connection Pool Exhaustion**: A slow analytics query in the Reporting module consumes all 50 HikariCP/SQLAlchemy connections, stalling Checkout.
- **Noisy Neighbor CPU/Memory**: Unbounded in-memory caching or image processing in one module triggers an OOMKill for the entire binary.
- **Eventual Consistency Without Durability**: Using an in-memory-only event bus (like plain `EventEmitter`) drops events if the pod restarts mid-dispatch.

## Production hardening

Make the modular monolith resilient and extraction-ready:

- **Per-Module Bulkheads**: Separate thread pools or async worker queues for heavy background modules so interactive HTTP handlers are never starved.
- **Durable Outbox Table**: Persist in-process domain events to an `event_publication` table so failed listeners retry automatically on restart.
- **Extraction Trigger**: Extract a module to a microservice only when it hits a concrete scaling, compliance, or team-autonomy wall—not on speculation.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Structure top-level packages by business capability, never by technical layer.
- [ ] Enforce module encapsulation and acyclicity in CI with ArchUnit, Packwerk, or `import-linter`.
- [ ] Isolate tables into per-module database schemas with zero cross-schema foreign keys.
- [ ] Pass immutable DTOs/events across module facades; never expose ORM entities.
- [ ] Back cross-module async events with a durable transactional outbox table.

interviewProblems.title: Modular Monolith Design
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Modular Monolith Design. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Structure a single deployable binary into strictly isolated domain modules with enforced public APIs and private schemas—gaining clean boundaries without network tax.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: In-Process Outbox Bus applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Inventory Module + DB.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Inventory Module + DB experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Fail the CI build automatically using ArchUnit (`@ApplicationModuleTest`), Packwerk, or `import-linter` rules.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Enforce module boundaries at compile/test time (ArchUnit, Spring Modulith, import-linter) and isolate database schemas so any module can be extracted into a microservice later in days, not months.
Avoid trap: Grouping code into `models/`, `services/`, and `controllers/` at the top level instead of domain module folders.
Avoid trap: Returning JPA/SQLAlchemy ORM entities from a module's public facade instead of immutable DTOs.
When to reach for it: Engineering organizations of 5–60 developers building a rich domain where boundaries are still evolving.
When to reach for it: Core workflows benefit from single-database ACID transactions and low-latency (<1 ms) cross-module reads without network serialization.

putItTogether.title: Putting Modular Monolith Design Together
putItTogether.summary: Enforce module boundaries at compile/test time (ArchUnit, Spring Modulith, import-linter) and isolate database schemas so any module can be extracted into a microservice later in days, not months.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Modular Monolith Design before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Using Packwerk to enforce explicit package boundaries and private constants allowed 1,000+ developers to ship safely in one deployable unit while selectively extracting only high-scale edges.
